lessons.title: Der, Die, Das — German Articles
lessons.explanation: German has three genders: masculine (der), feminine (die), and neuter (das), plus plural (die). Every noun has a grammatical gender that must be memorized. Example: der Mann (the man), die Frau (the woman), das Kind (the child).
examples: der Hund (the dog - masc.)
die Katze (the cat - fem.)
das Buch (the book - neut.)
die Kinder (the children - pl.)
lessons.tip: Always learn German nouns with their article: not just Tisch, but der Tisch.

quiz.question: What article does 'Kind' (child, neuter) take?
Which article is used for plural nouns?

lessons.title: Personal Pronouns
lessons.explanation: German personal pronouns: ich (I), du (you-informal), er (he), sie (she), es (it), wir (we), ihr (you-plural), Sie (you-formal), sie (they).
examples: Ich bin Schüler. (I am a student.)
Du bist mein Freund. (You are my friend.)
Er spricht Deutsch. (He speaks German.)
Wir lernen Grammatik. (We are learning grammar.)
lessons.tip: Note that 'sie' can mean 'she', 'they', or 'you (formal)' depending on context and capitalization.

quiz.question: How do you say 'I' in German?
Which pronoun means 'we'?

lessons.title: Sein — To Be
lessons.explanation: The verb 'sein' (to be) is irregular: ich bin, du bist, er/sie/es ist, wir sind, ihr seid, sie/Sie sind.
examples: Ich bin müde. (I am tired.)
Du bist klug. (You are smart.)
Er ist Lehrer. (He is a teacher.)
Wir sind glücklich. (We are happy.)
lessons.tip: Sein is used for permanent characteristics, identities, and locations.

quiz.question: How do you say 'she is' in German?
What does 'wir sind' mean?

lessons.title: Haben — To Have
lessons.explanation: The verb 'haben' (to have): ich habe, du hast, er/sie/es hat, wir haben, ihr habt, sie/Sie haben.
examples: Ich habe einen Bruder. (I have a brother.)
Du hast Hunger. (You are hungry.)
Sie hat ein Auto. (She has a car.)
Wir haben Zeit. (We have time.)
lessons.tip: Haben is used to form the past tense (Perfekt) of most verbs in German.

quiz.question: How do you say 'I have' in German?

lessons.title: Cases — Nominative and Accusative
lessons.explanation: German has four cases (Nominative, Accusative, Dative, Genitive) that show the role of a noun. Nominative = subject (who does the action). Accusative = direct object (what receives the action). Der changes to den in accusative masculine.
examples: Der Hund beißt den Mann. (The dog bites the man.)
Ich sehe den Lehrer. (I see the teacher.)
Die Frau kauft das Buch. (The woman buys the book.)
Er liebt die Musik. (He loves music.)
lessons.tip: Only masculine 'der' changes to 'den' in accusative. Die and das stay the same.

quiz.question: What happens to 'der' (masc.) in the accusative case?

lessons.title: Word Order — Verb Second
lessons.explanation: In German main clauses, the conjugated verb is ALWAYS in second position. If something other than the subject starts the sentence, the verb stays second and the subject moves after it (inversion).
examples: Ich gehe heute ins Kino. (I go to the cinema today.)
Heute gehe ich ins Kino. (Today I go to the cinema.)
Morgen spielen wir Fußball. (Tomorrow we play football.)
Er kommt um drei Uhr. (He comes at three o'clock.)
lessons.tip: Count the verb position — it must always be #2 in a main clause no matter what comes first.

quiz.question: In a German main clause, the verb is always in position:

lessons.title: Separable Verbs — Trennbare Verben
lessons.explanation: Many German verbs have a separable prefix (an-, auf-, aus-, mit-, zu-, ein-, etc.) that detaches from the verb and moves to the end of the clause in a conjugated main clause. In the infinitive the prefix stays attached, e.g. aufstehen (to get up).
examples: Ich stehe um sechs Uhr auf. (I get up at six o'clock.)
Er macht das Fenster auf. (He opens the window.)
Wir rufen dich später an. (We will call you later.)
Sie räumt ihr Zimmer auf. (She tidies up her room.)
lessons.tip: In the infinitive the prefix is attached (aufstehen), but in a conjugated main clause it splits off and goes to the very end.

quiz.question: Where does the separable prefix go in a present-tense main clause?
options: at the end of the clause

quiz.question: What is the infinitive form of 'steht ... auf'?

lessons.title: Possessive Adjectives — Mein, Dein, Sein…
lessons.explanation: German possessive adjectives (mein, dein, sein, ihr, unser, euer, ihr/Ihr) take the same endings as 'ein' and agree with the gender, case, and number of the noun they describe, not with the possessor's gender.
examples: mein Bruder (my brother — masc.)
meine Schwester (my sister — fem.)
sein Auto (his car)
ihre Tasche (her bag)
lessons.tip: Possessive adjectives follow the same ending pattern as 'ein' — learn ein-word endings and apply them to all possessives.

quiz.question: Which possessive means 'her' in German?
What ending does 'mein' take before a feminine noun in the nominative?

lessons.title: Modal Verbs — können, müssen, wollen
lessons.explanation: Modal verbs modify the meaning of the main verb. Key modals: können (can/able to), müssen (must/have to), wollen (want to), sollen (should), dürfen (may/allowed to), mögen (like). The main verb goes to the END of the sentence in infinitive form.
examples: Ich kann Deutsch sprechen. (I can speak German.)
Du musst die Hausaufgaben machen. (You must do the homework.)
Er will nach Berlin fahren. (He wants to go to Berlin.)
Wir dürfen hier nicht parken. (We are not allowed to park here.)
lessons.tip: Modal verb is conjugated in position 2; the infinitive main verb goes to the very end.

quiz.question: Where does the main infinitive verb go when a modal is used?

lessons.title: Dative Case
lessons.explanation: The dative case marks the indirect object (to/for whom something is done) and follows dative prepositions (aus, bei, mit, nach, seit, von, zu) and dative verbs (helfen, danken, gefallen). Article changes: der→dem, die→der, das→dem, die (pl.)→den (+n on the plural noun).
examples: Ich gebe dem Mann das Buch. (I give the man the book.)
Sie hilft ihrer Mutter. (She helps her mother.)
Wir fahren mit dem Bus. (We travel by bus.)
Das Geschenk gehört den Kindern. (The gift belongs to the children.)
lessons.tip: Remember the dative prepositions with the mnemonic 'aus, bei, mit, nach, seit, von, zu' — they always trigger dative.

quiz.question: What does 'die' (fem., nominative) become in the dative?
Which preposition always takes the dative?

lessons.title: Perfekt — Present Perfect Tense
lessons.explanation: The Perfekt is the most common past tense in spoken German, formed with haben or sein (conjugated) plus a past participle (ge-...-t/en) placed at the end of the clause. Most verbs use haben; verbs of motion or change of state use sein.
examples: Ich habe Pizza gegessen. (I have eaten pizza.)
Er ist nach Berlin gefahren. (He has traveled to Berlin.)
Wir haben einen Film gesehen. (We have watched a film.)
Sie ist früh aufgestanden. (She got up early.)
lessons.tip: Regular participles: ge + stem + t (machen→gemacht); irregular verbs often use ge + stem + en with a vowel change (sehen→gesehen).

quiz.question: Which auxiliary does 'fahren' (to travel) use in the Perfekt?
What is the past participle of 'machen'?

lessons.title: Genitive Case
lessons.explanation: The genitive case shows possession ('of the...' / 's) and follows certain prepositions (während, trotz, wegen, statt). Masculine and neuter nouns typically add -s or -es, with article changes: der→des, die→der, das→des, die (pl.)→der.
examples: das Auto des Mannes (the man's car)
die Farbe der Blume (the color of the flower)
wegen des Wetters (because of the weather)
das Buch des Kindes (the child's book)
lessons.tip: In everyday spoken German, 'von + dative' often replaces the genitive (das Auto von dem Mann), but the genitive is standard in writing.

quiz.question: What does 'der' (masc., nominative) become in the genitive?
Which preposition takes the genitive?

lessons.title: Subordinate Clauses — Verb-Final Rule
lessons.explanation: In subordinate clauses introduced by conjunctions (weil, dass, wenn, obwohl, damit…), the conjugated verb moves to the VERY END of the clause. This is the opposite of main clauses.
examples: Ich lerne Deutsch, weil es interessant ist. (I learn German because it is interesting.)
Er sagt, dass er müde ist. (He says that he is tired.)
Wenn ich Zeit habe, lese ich. (When I have time, I read.)
Obwohl es regnet, gehen wir spazieren. (Although it is raining, we go for a walk.)
lessons.tip: Remember: in subordinate clauses, conjugated verb = LAST.

quiz.question: In a German subordinate clause with 'weil', where does the verb go?

lessons.title: Konjunktiv II — Subjunctive II
lessons.explanation: Konjunktiv II expresses hypothetical, unreal, or polite situations ('would/could/if...then'). It is formed from the simple past stem plus an umlaut (for strong verbs) and endings, but most commonly with 'würde + infinitive' for weak verbs.
examples: Wenn ich Zeit hätte, würde ich kommen. (If I had time, I would come.)
Ich würde das gern machen. (I would like to do that.)
Könntest du mir helfen? (Could you help me?)
Wenn er reich wäre, würde er reisen. (If he were rich, he would travel.)
lessons.tip: For most verbs, use 'würde + infinitive'; only common verbs like sein (wäre), haben (hätte), and the modals keep their own Konjunktiv II forms.

quiz.question: Which construction is most common for forming Konjunktiv II with regular verbs?
What is the Konjunktiv II 'ich' form of 'sein'?

lessons.title: Passiv — Passive Voice
lessons.explanation: The passive voice shifts focus to the recipient of an action rather than the doer, formed with werden (conjugated) plus the past participle. The agent, if mentioned, is introduced with 'von' + dative.
examples: Das Haus wird gebaut. (The house is being built.)
Der Brief wurde von ihr geschrieben. (The letter was written by her.)
Die Tür wird geöffnet. (The door is opened.)
Das Auto wurde repariert. (The car was repaired.)
lessons.tip: Don't confuse the Vorgangspassiv (werden + participle, an action) with the Zustandspassiv (sein + participle, a resulting state).

quiz.question: Which verb is used as the auxiliary to form the German passive?
How do you introduce the agent (the 'doer') in a passive sentence?

lessons.title: Relativsätze — Relative Clauses
lessons.explanation: German relative clauses use relative pronouns (der, die, das, etc.) that match the gender and number of their antecedent but take their case from their grammatical role inside the relative clause. Since it is a subordinate clause, the conjugated verb moves to the end.
examples: Der Mann, der dort steht, ist mein Lehrer. (The man who is standing there is my teacher.)
Die Frau, die ich kenne, wohnt in Berlin. (The woman whom I know lives in Berlin.)
Das Buch, das ich lese, ist spannend. (The book that I am reading is exciting.)
Der Freund, dem ich vertraue, hilft mir immer. (The friend whom I trust always helps me.)
lessons.tip: Relative pronouns look like definite articles but decline like 'der/die/das' — check the noun's gender for the pronoun and its grammatical role for the case.

quiz.question: In 'Der Mann, der dort steht...', what determines the case of 'der'?
options: its role within the relative clause

quiz.question: Where does the conjugated verb go in a German relative clause?
